summary.text: For each prime \(p\), the numerator and denominator have valuations \(\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor^2\) and \(\sum_{i\ge1}S(\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor)\), respectively, where \(S(m)=\sum_{k=1}^m k\lfloor m/k\rfloor\). Since \(S(m)\le m^2\), with equality exactly for \(m\le2\) and strict inequality for \(m\ge3\), the quotient has positive \(p\)-adic valuation exactly when \(\lfloor n/p\rfloor\ge3\), equivalently \(p\le\lfloor n/3\rfloor\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N(n)=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\prod_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(j,k),
\qquad
D(n)=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left(\left\lfloor\frac nk\right\rfloor !\right)^k.
\]
Thus the sequence in the statement is defined by the natural-number quotient
\[
a(n)=\frac{N(n)}{D(n)}.
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is exact, and then determine precisely when a given prime divides it.

For a prime \(p\) and a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in the prime factorization of \(x\). We use the elementary facts
\[
v_p(xy)=v_p(x)+v_p(y),\qquad v_p(x^r)=r v_p(x),
\]
and
\[
v_p(x!)=\sum_{i\ge 1}\left\lfloor\frac{x}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
The latter is Legendre’s formula: each multiple of \(p\) among \(1,\dots,x\) contributes at least one factor of \(p\), each multiple of \(p^2\) contributes one additional factor, and so on.

We will also repeatedly use the fact that the number of multiples of a positive integer \(q\) in \(\{1,\dots,n\}\) is \(\lfloor n/q\rfloor\).

Define, for every nonnegative integer \(m\),
\[
S(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{m} k\left\lfloor\frac{m}{k}\right\rfloor.
\]
We first establish the simple but decisive estimates
\[
S(m)\le m^2\quad\text{for every }m\ge0,
\]
with equality exactly for \(m=0,1,2\), and hence
\[
S(m)<m^2\quad\text{for every }m\ge3.
\]
Indeed, for each \(1\le k\le m\),
\[
k\left\lfloor\frac mk\right\rfloor\le m.
\]
There are \(m\) summands, so summing gives \(S(m)\le m^2\). Directly,
\[
S(0)=0,
\qquad S(1)=1,
\qquad S(2)=1\cdot2+2\cdot1=4,
\]
so equality holds for \(m\le2\). If \(m\ge3\), all the summands are still at most \(m\), but the summand with \(k=m-1\) is strictly smaller than \(m\), because
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{m}{m-1}\right\rfloor=1
\]
and therefore that summand is \(m-1<m\). Thus the whole sum is strictly less than the sum of \(m\) copies of \(m\), proving \(S(m)<m^2\).

We now compute the valuation of the numerator. For positive \(j,k\),
\[
v_p(\gcd(j,k))
 =\#\{i\ge1:p^i\mid j\text{ and }p^i\mid k\}.
\]
This is because \(p^i\) divides \(\gcd(j,k)\) exactly when it divides both \(j\) and \(k\), and the number of positive powers \(p^i\) dividing a positive integer is its \(p\)-adic valuation. Hence, after summing over all ordered pairs \((j,k)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(N(n))
&=\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^n v_p(\gcd(j,k))\\
&=\sum_{i\ge1}
 \#\{j\le n:p^i\mid j\}\,
 \#\{k\le n:p^i\mid k\}\\
&=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
All but finitely many terms vanish. In particular, it is enough to sum over \(1\le i\le n\). To see this uniformly, a prime satisfies \(p\ge2\), and therefore
\(p^{n+1}\ge2^{n+1}>n\); consequently \(p^i>n\) for all \(i\ge n+1\). Thus
\[
\boxed{
 v_p(N(n))=\sum_{i=1}^{n}
 \left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2.}
\tag{1}
\]

Next compute the valuation of the denominator. By the product and power rules for valuations and Legendre’s formula,
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(D(n))
&=\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\,
 v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac nk\right\rfloor!\right)\\
&=\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\sum_{i\ge1}
 \left\lfloor
 \frac{\lfloor n/k\rfloor}{p^i}
 \right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
For positive integers \(k,p^i\), successive integer division satisfies
\[
\left\lfloor
 \frac{\lfloor n/k\rfloor}{p^i}
\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{n}{kp^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor
\frac{\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor}{k}
\right\rfloor.
\]
Interchanging the two finite sums therefore gives
\[
v_p(D(n))
=\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^{n}
 k\left\lfloor
 \frac{\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor}{k}
 \right\rfloor.
\]
Put
\[
m_i=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
If \(k>m_i\), then \(\lfloor m_i/k\rfloor=0\), so the inner sum may be truncated at \(m_i\). It is therefore exactly \(S(m_i)\). Again, terms with \(i>n\) vanish, and we obtain
\[
\boxed{
 v_p(D(n))=\sum_{i=1}^{n}
 S\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^i}\right\rfloor\right).}
\tag{2}
\]

Before studying divisibility by a particular prime, we verify that \(D(n)\) really divides \(N(n)\). Let \(q\) be any prime and put
\[
r_i=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
By (1), (2), and the inequality \(S(r_i)\le r_i^2\),
\[
v_q(D(n))
 =\sum_{i=1}^{n}S(r_i)
 \le\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_i^2
 =v_q(N(n)).
\]
Both \(N(n)\) and \(D(n)\) are positive: every gcd occurring in \(N(n)\) is positive, and every factorial occurring in \(D(n)\) is positive. Since the exponent of every prime in \(D(n)\) is at most its exponent in \(N(n)\), unique prime factorization implies
\[
D(n)\mid N(n).
\]
Consequently the natural-number quotient defining \(a(n)\) is the ordinary exact positive integer quotient, and
\[
N(n)=a(n)D(n).
\]
Taking \(p\)-adic valuations yields
\[
v_p(N(n))=v_p(a(n))+v_p(D(n)).
\]
Thus
\[
p\mid a(n)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
v_p(a(n))\ge1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
v_p(D(n))<v_p(N(n)).
\tag{3}
\]

It remains to determine exactly when this last strict inequality occurs. Fix the prime \(p\), and continue to write
\[
m_i=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Equations (1) and (2) say
\[
v_p(N(n))=\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_i^2,
\qquad
v_p(D(n))=\sum_{i=1}^{n}S(m_i).
\]
For every \(i\), we know \(S(m_i)\le m_i^2\). Hence the denominator valuation is strictly less than the numerator valuation exactly when at least one of these termwise inequalities is strict.

The sequence \((m_i)\) is nonincreasing, since \(p^i\ge p\) for every \(i\ge1\). Therefore
\[
m_i\le m_1=\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor.
\]
If \(m_1\le2\), then every \(m_i\le2\), and for such values we proved \(S(m_i)=m_i^2\). Every summand in the two valuation formulas is then equal, so
\[
v_p(D(n))=v_p(N(n)).
\]
Conversely, if \(m_1\ge3\), then the \(i=1\) summand is strictly smaller on the denominator side:
\[
S(m_1)<m_1^2.
\]
All remaining denominator summands are at most their corresponding numerator summands. Since \(n>0\), the index \(i=1\) is present in the sums, and it follows that
\[
v_p(D(n))<v_p(N(n)).
\]
We have therefore proved
\[
v_p(D(n))<v_p(N(n))
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
3\le\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor.
\tag{4}
\]

Finally, because \(p>0\), the standard relation between integer division and multiplication gives
\[
3\le\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
3p\le n.
\]
Likewise,
\[
p\le\left\lfloor\frac n3\right\rfloor
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
3p\le n.
\]
Thus
\[
3\le\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p\le\left\lfloor\frac n3\right\rfloor.
\tag{5}
\]
Combining (3), (4), and (5), we conclude that for every positive integer \(n\) and every prime \(p\),
\[
\boxed{
 p\mid a(n)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 p\le\left\lfloor\frac n3\right\rfloor.}
\]
This is the desired conjecture.
